column1: In causal set theory, what gives volume?
column2: Counting elements: number gives volume, order gives causal structure (Dowker 2005, §2.3).

column1: At what scale is spacetime proposed to be discrete?
column2: Of the order of the Planck scale (Dowker 2005, §2.3).
The conjecture that two continuum spacetimes approximating the same causal set are close to each other (Dowker 2005, §2.3).

column1: What does Dowker identify with the passage of time?
column2: The birth of spacetime atoms: the present is the process of birth (Dowker 2014).
Growth by births that are only partly ordered; Dowker credits the term to Sorkin (Dowker 2014).

column1: Is the birth order of spacetime atoms physical?
column2: Only where it shows in the causal order; labels are pure gauge, the discrete analogue of general covariance (Dowker 2014; Rideout & Sorkin 1999, §3).

column1: Who are the "Blockheads", and Dowker's reply?
column2: Those who run growth to infinity and call the result a static block. Reply: that is a different theory, fitting experience less well (Dowker 2014).

column1: In sequential growth, does growth happen in time?
column2: No: it is taken to constitute time, not happen in it (Rideout & Sorkin 1999, §1.1).
No: every element has a descendant, a result of Henson's (Dowker 2005, §3.4).

column1: Crystallizing block: what is fixed and what is open?
column2: The past is fixed; the future does not yet exist physically; the present is where quantum outcomes become definite (Ellis & Rothman 2010).

column1: What does Rovelli put in place of time?
column2: Relations between variables; time returns statistically as "thermal time" (Rovelli 2009, §IV, §VI).

column1: Why can a universe of massless particles not keep time?
column2: Massless particles experience no passage of time, so nothing can be built into a clock (Penrose 2006, p. 2).
